study.title: Fêtes d'hiver
study.question: How do francophone Canadians celebrate winter?
study.passage:
Background (written for this lesson from public sources):
Le Festival du Voyageur: held every February in Saint-Boniface, Winnipeg's French quarter, since 1970. It celebrates the voyageurs, the Métis and francophone history of western Canada. Activities: snow sculptures, fiddle music and jigging, a beard-growing contest, sugar shack treats, and the festival cry "Hé ho !" Typical food: soupe aux pois, tourtière, tire sur la neige.
Le Carnaval de Québec: one of the world's largest winter carnivals, held in Québec City in late January and February; it has run every year since 1955, with earlier carnivals dating back to 1894. Its mascot, Bonhomme Carnaval, wears a red tuque and a ceinture fléchée (arrow sash). Activities: the ice palace, night parades, snow baths, and a famous canoe race across the icy St. Lawrence River.
Text: Au Festival du Voyageur, on écoute du violon, on mange de la soupe aux pois et on crie « Hé ho ! ». Au Carnaval de Québec, on visite le palais de glace de Bonhomme et on regarde la course en canot sur le fleuve Saint-Laurent.
Activity: groups make a fact sheet for one festival: où, quand, depuis quand, pourquoi, activités, nourriture, symboles.
study.source: Summary from public sources about the Festival du Voyageur and the Carnaval de Québec.

body.objective: Students will be able to compare celebrations.
successCriteria: I can describe francophone celebrations from different countries
I can compare celebrations using comparatives

body.hook: Bastille Day in France, la Fête nationale in Quebec, Kanaval in Haiti, la Fête de la musique: francophone celebrations range from national holidays to street parties. How do they compare with each other, and with yours?

study.title: Comparer les fêtes
study.question: How do francophone celebrations compare?
study.passage:
Celebrations (written for this lesson from public sources):
Le 14 juillet (France): la Fête nationale, often called Bastille Day in English, marks the 1789 storming of the Bastille. Military parade in Paris, fireworks, dances.
Le 24 juin (Québec): la Fête nationale du Québec (Saint-Jean-Baptiste): bonfires, concerts, blue-and-white flags.
Le 15 août (Acadie): Fête nationale de l'Acadie: the Tintamarre, a noisy parade with pots and pans.
Kanaval (Haïti): carnival before Lent, with costumes, music and parades.
La Fête de la musique (21 juin, France, since 1982, now worldwide): free music in the streets on the longest day.
Comparatives: Le Carnaval de Québec est plus froid que le Kanaval. La Fête de la musique est moins officielle que le 14 juillet. Le Tintamarre est aussi bruyant qu'un concert !
Activity: groups compare two celebrations on a chart (date, origin, activities, food, symbols), then write five comparative sentences and one sentence about what each celebration shows about the culture.
study.source: Summary from public sources about francophone celebrations.

body.objective: Students will be able to present a francophone celebration.
body.iCan: I can present a francophone celebration.
successCriteria: I can research and present a francophone celebration in French
I can use the present, passé composé and futur proche in one presentation
I can answer audience questions in French
body.hook: Your final French 9 project: become an expert on one francophone celebration and present it so vividly that your audience can almost hear the music and taste the food.

study.title: Présente une fête
study.question: How do I present a francophone celebration in French?
study.passage:
Project guide (written for this lesson):
Choose a celebration: Festival du Voyageur, Carnaval de Québec, Fête nationale du Québec, Tintamarre, 14 juillet, Kanaval, Fête de la musique, Rendez-vous de la Francophonie (March, across Canada), le temps des sucres, la Chandeleur, or another with teacher approval.
Content (3 minutes): 1. Introduction: name, place, date (present). 2. History: how it began (passé composé: La fête a commencé en…). 3. Activities, food, music and symbols (present: chaque année, on…). 4. A comparison with a celebration you know (plus/moins/aussi … que). 5. Your plan: Un jour, je vais aller… (futur proche).
Visuals: slides or a poster with images and key words (no long sentences).
Speaking tips: practise pronunciation, look at the audience, speak slowly.
Questions: each presenter answers two questions: Quand est la fête ? Qu'est-ce qu'on mange ? Pourquoi est-ce important ?
Rubric: content, three tenses used correctly, vocabulary, pronunciation, visuals, answering questions.
study.source: Original project written for this lesson.
steps: Use present, passé composé and futur proche
discussion: Why did you choose your celebration?

study.product: Present a three-minute presentation on a francophone celebration using three tenses, a comparison and visuals, and answer two questions in French.
